name: NVIDIA H200 SXM 141GB (GH100, compute capability 9.0)
notes: Published figures, not a measurement: no device run has confirmed any of them, and none has run here. launch_ns, link_ns, memory_efficiency, occupancy_to_saturate and memory_latency_ns are assumptions, the same on every packaged card, marked as such below.

documents.datasheet: NVIDIA H200 Tensor Core GPU datasheet, the H200 SXM column, preliminary specifications (https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/b2kt2580e5b6424if22lg65223m6ghjb.pdf, linked from https://resources.nvidia.com/en-us-hopper-architecture/nvidia-h100-tensor-c)
documents.overview: NVIDIA, CUDA Programming and Optimization (2024), the NVIDIA H200 SXM overview (https://developer-blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/CUDA-Programming-and-Optimization.pdf)
documents.guide: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2, Compute Capabilities, Tables 30 and 31 (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html)

source.sms: NVIDIA's CUDA Programming and Optimization overview of the H200 SXM: 132 SMs, each with 128 FP32 cores, 64 FP64 cores and 64 INT32 cores.
source.ghz: Derived: the datasheet's FP32 67 TFLOPS on 132 x 128 cores at 2 operations per fused multiply-add is 1.98 GHz, the H100 SXM5's published FP32 boost clock. NVIDIA publishes no H200 clock.
source.dram_gbps: Datasheet: GPU memory bandwidth 4.8 TB/s (HBM3e, 141 GB).
source.flops: Datasheet: FP32 67 TFLOPS, FP64 34 TFLOPS. i32 is derived as the other cards' is: 64 INT32 cores an SM, 2 operations each a clock, at 1.98 GHz on 132 SMs.
source.tensor: Datasheet, whose tensor figures are with sparsity; dense is half: TF32 989/2, BFLOAT16 and FP16 1,979/2, FP8 3,958/2 TFLOPS. The model reads tensor_f16; the others are recorded for a reader.
source.link_gbps: Datasheet: PCIe Gen5 128 GB/s, both directions together, so 64 GB/s each way, before protocol overhead.
source.occupancy: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2, Compute Capabilities, Tables 30 and 31 (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html), 9.0 column: an SM holds 64 K registers, 64 warps (2048 threads), 32 blocks and 228 KB of shared memory, and a block at most 1024 threads, 64 K registers, 255 registers a thread and 227 KB of shared memory, past 48 KB only by opting in. The CUDA C++ Programming Guide 12.9, section 20, says for each of 8.x, 9.0, 10.x and 12.0 that the 1 KB of shared memory not made available to a thread block is reserved for system use (shared_reserved). CUDA 13.2's occupancy calculator, cuda_occupancy.h, allocates registers a warp at a time in units of 256 (register_unit) from each of the 4 parts of the register file (partitions) and shared memory in units of 128 bytes (shared_unit), and gives compute capability 9.0 the same 32 blocks an SM; tools/checks/occupancy.py holds the card's resident blocks to that calculator (evidence/v1_2/occupancy).
source.shared_bytes_per_clock: CUDA C++ Programming Guide: shared memory has 32 banks, each 32 bits wide a clock cycle.
source.memory_latency_ns: Assumed. NVIDIA publishes no device-memory latency and no run here has measured one; it prices only a pipeline's asynchronous copies, as the bytes in flight over this latency. Every packaged card assumes the same 500 ns.
